HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)  -- Zimbabwe police arrested on Friday a magistrate who ordered the release of a senior opposition politician granted bail by the country's High Court, a lawyer said. A Zimbabwean policeman patrols outside the entrance of Mutare Magistrates court. The order to release the politician had been suspended when state lawyers appealed the HIgh Court decision. Trust Maanda, a lawyer in Mutare city about 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of Harare, told CNN by phone that magistrate Livingstone Chipadze had been arrested. "He is in police custody. The police are saying he ordered the release of Roy Bennett in compliance with the High Court ruling," said Maanda. Bennett is the choice of the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) for deputy agriculture minister under the power-sharing government formed last month. On Wednesday, Chipadze ordered Bennett be released from a prison in Mutare as had been ruled by the High Court last week. However, that order, which required Bennett to post $2,000 as bail, was suspended after the state filed an appeal with Zimbabwe's Supreme Court. "I can confirm the arrest, but I will be in position to tell you the charge he will face later," said a police official in Mutare over the phone. "He is likely to go to court on Saturday or Monday. But most magistrates here [in Mutare] have gone on strike over his arrest." Chipadze joins Bennett in prison in Mutare. Bennett was arrested on February 13 and is facing charges of possessing arms for the purposes of banditry, terrorism and sabotage. The continued detention of Bennett, an ally of MDC leader and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai, is seen by many as a crack in the foundation of the coalition Tsvangirai formed with President Robert Mugabe. Meanwhile, a Zimbabwe High Court judge Friday ordered the immediate release of three human rights activists in state "safe custody" to testify against human rights activist Jestina Mukoko, who is facing charges of plotting to topple Mugabe. Opposition MDC activists Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona have been missing since October last year after they were abducted from their homes under the cover of darkness. Lawyers Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda took the state to the High Court in an attempt to win the release the trio. But the state represented by Nelson Mutsonziwa had opposed the application, saying the three would be state witnesses when the trial of Mukoko starts. The MDC lawyers then successfully argued that the three were bread winners for their families and the state had not provided their families with assistance while they are in custody. Delivering the judgment, Justice Ben Hlatswayo said, "I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal." Relatives of the three who were milling around the High Court could not hide their joy after Mhike told them of Hlatswayo's ruling.

HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN) — A lawyer said Friday that police in Zimbabwe had taken into custody a magistrate who directed that a senior opposition figure be freed after the politician was granted bail by the nation’s High Court.

A Zimbabwean police officer was seen on patrol outside the entrance to the Mutare Magistrates Court.

The release order had been put on hold after government lawyers challenged the High Court’s decision. Trust Maanda, an attorney based in Mutare, about 300 kilometers (186 miles) east of Harare, told CNN by telephone that Magistrate Livingstone Chipadze had been arrested.

“He is in police custody. The police are saying he ordered the release of Roy Bennett in compliance with the High Court ruling,” Maanda said.

Bennett had been selected by the opposition Movement for Democratic Change (MDC) to serve as deputy agriculture minister in the power-sharing administration created the previous month.

On Wednesday, Chipadze instructed that Bennett be freed from a prison in Mutare, following the High Court’s ruling from the week before. But that decision, which set Bennett’s bail at $2,000, was suspended once the state appealed to Zimbabwe’s Supreme Court.

A police official in Mutare confirmed the arrest by phone, saying, “I can confirm the arrest, but I will be in position to tell you the charge he will face later.”

“He is likely to go to court on Saturday or Monday. But most magistrates here [in Mutare] have gone on strike over his arrest,” the official added.

Chipadze was placed in the same Mutare prison where Bennett is being held. Bennett was detained on February 13 and faces accusations of possessing weapons for purposes of banditry, terrorism and sabotage.

Many observers view Bennett’s continued imprisonment as a sign of strain in the coalition government formed by MDC leader and Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai with President Robert Mugabe. Bennett is an ally of Tsvangirai.

Separately, on Friday, a Zimbabwe High Court judge ordered that three human rights activists being held in state “safe custody” be released immediately. The three had been expected to testify against human rights campaigner Jestina Mukoko, who is accused of plotting to overthrow Mugabe.

MDC activists Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona had not been seen since October of the previous year, after being taken from their homes at night.

Attorneys Chris Mhike and Innocent Chagonda brought the matter before the High Court in an effort to secure the release of the three men. The state, represented by Nelson Mutsonziwa, opposed the request, arguing that the men would serve as prosecution witnesses when Mukoko’s trial began.

Lawyers for the MDC countered successfully that the three men were the primary earners for their families and that the government had not helped support those families while the men remained detained.

In issuing his ruling, Justice Ben Hlatswayo said: “I order the immediate release of Fannie Tembo, Lloyd Tarumbwa and Terry Musona from police custody or the custody of any other state agent. This order stands enforceable notwithstanding the noting or filing of an appeal.”

Family members of the three men, who had gathered around the High Court, were visibly overjoyed after Mhike informed them of Hlatswayo’s decision.

**Zimbabwe police arrest magistrate after bail ruling for MDC politician Roy Bennett**

**Mutare, Zimbabwe** — Zimbabwean police arrested a magistrate in the eastern city of Mutare after he ordered the release on bail of Roy Bennett, a senior official in Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai’s Movement for Democratic Change, according to lawyers and party officials.

Magistrate Livingstone Chipadza had granted Bennett bail after the MDC politician was detained on charges linked to allegations of terrorism, insurgency and sabotage — accusations Bennett and his supporters have denied as politically motivated.

Bennett, a former white commercial farmer and longtime critic of President Robert Mugabe, had been nominated by Tsvangirai to serve as deputy agriculture minister in Zimbabwe’s fragile power-sharing government. His arrest came just as the unity administration between Mugabe’s ZANU-PF and Tsvangirai’s MDC was attempting to take shape after months of political crisis following disputed elections.

The detention of the magistrate who ordered Bennett’s release has raised new concerns among lawyers and human rights groups about the independence of Zimbabwe’s judiciary and the continued use of state security institutions against perceived opponents of Mugabe’s party.

Bennett’s case has become an early test of the coalition government, which was formed after regional mediation efforts sought to end the turmoil that followed the 2008 presidential election. Tsvangirai won the first round of that vote, but pulled out of the runoff, citing widespread violence against MDC supporters. Mugabe, who had ruled Zimbabwe since independence in 1980, remained president under the power-sharing deal, while Tsvangirai became prime minister.

Human rights activists have said Bennett’s arrest fits a broader pattern of intimidation targeting opposition figures, civic leaders and rights defenders. Among the most prominent cases was that of Jestina Mukoko, a human rights campaigner who was abducted and detained in late 2008 before facing charges the government said were related to attempts to recruit people for military training. Mukoko denied the allegations, and rights organizations condemned her treatment.

Other activists and MDC members were also detained during the same period, prompting demands from Tsvangirai’s party that political prisoners be released as a condition for rebuilding trust in the unity government.

The arrest of the Mutare magistrate underscored the continuing tensions between Zimbabwe’s rival political camps. MDC officials have accused hardliners in the security services and justice system of trying to undermine the new government before it can function. ZANU-PF officials have maintained that criminal matters should proceed through the courts and have rejected claims that prosecutions are politically directed.

Bennett has long been a symbolic figure in Zimbabwe’s opposition movement. He was previously jailed after a confrontation in parliament and became a vocal critic of Mugabe’s land-reform program, which redistributed white-owned commercial farms to Black Zimbabweans but was blamed by critics for contributing to a collapse in agricultural production and food shortages.

The unity government was intended to stabilize Zimbabwe after years of economic decline, hyperinflation and political repression. But the detention of Bennett — and now the arrest of the magistrate who granted him bail — has fueled doubts about whether Mugabe and Tsvangirai can share power while key institutions remain divided.

**Zimbabwe crisis deepens after magistrate arrested for granting bail to opposition figure Roy Bennett**

**HARARE, Zimbabwe (CNN)** — Zimbabwe’s fragile political transition was thrown into deeper turmoil after authorities arrested a magistrate who had ordered the release of opposition politician Roy Bennett in compliance with a High Court bail ruling, raising fresh concerns about judicial independence and the rule of law in the country.

Bennett, a senior official in the Movement for Democratic Change (MDC), has been at the center of a politically charged case that has intensified tensions between President Robert Mugabe’s ZANU-PF party and the MDC, led by Prime Minister Morgan Tsvangirai.

The magistrate’s arrest came shortly after Bennett was granted bail by the High Court, a decision that should have cleared the way for his release. Instead, the legal proceedings triggered a new confrontation between the courts and state security officials, with critics accusing authorities of using the criminal justice system to intimidate judges, magistrates and opposition leaders.

The arrest has deepened fears that Zimbabwe’s power-sharing government — formed after months of violence, disputed elections and international pressure — remains vulnerable to interference from security forces and hard-liners loyal to Mugabe.

### Opposition says arrest is political intimidation

MDC officials condemned the magistrate’s arrest, calling it an attack on the judiciary and a direct challenge to the authority of the High Court.

Party representatives said the move demonstrated that Zimbabwe’s courts were operating under political pressure and that state institutions remained stacked against the opposition despite the formation of a unity government.

Bennett, a former white commercial farmer and outspoken Mugabe critic, had been nominated to serve as deputy agriculture minister in the unity government. His arrest and continued legal troubles have become a major point of contention between the MDC and ZANU-PF.

The MDC has argued that the prosecution of Bennett is politically motivated and designed to prevent him from taking up his government post.

### Bennett case tests unity government

Bennett was arrested on allegations linked to terrorism, banditry and insurgency — charges he has denied. His supporters say the accusations are part of a broader pattern of harassment against MDC officials and activists.

The case has become one of the most visible tests of Zimbabwe’s power-sharing deal, which brought Mugabe and Tsvangirai into the same government after the violent and disputed 2008 elections.

Under that agreement, Mugabe remained president while Tsvangirai became prime minister. The arrangement was intended to end Zimbabwe’s political deadlock and stabilize an economy devastated by hyperinflation, food shortages and mass unemployment.

But the unity government has struggled from the start, with disputes over senior appointments, control of security services, media freedom and the prosecution of opposition figures.

### Rule of law under scrutiny

Legal analysts and human rights groups said the arrest of a magistrate for carrying out a superior court’s order could have far-reaching consequences.

They warned that it may discourage judicial officers from issuing rulings unfavorable to the state, particularly in politically sensitive cases.

Zimbabwe’s judiciary has long been accused by rights organizations and opposition parties of being vulnerable to executive pressure, especially in cases involving land seizures, election disputes and opposition activists.

The Bennett case has renewed scrutiny of whether court rulings are being respected by police, prosecutors and security agencies.

### Regional pressure likely to grow

The crisis is also likely to draw attention from regional leaders in the Southern African Development Community, known as SADC, which helped broker Zimbabwe’s power-sharing agreement.

South Africa, Zimbabwe’s most influential neighbor, has repeatedly urged the unity government to resolve disputes through negotiation. But rights groups have criticized regional leaders for being too cautious in confronting Mugabe over alleged abuses.

Western governments, including the United States and Britain, have maintained targeted sanctions against Mugabe and senior ZANU-PF figures, citing human rights violations and the collapse of democratic institutions.

Those governments have said they want to see clear evidence of political reform before normalizing relations or expanding direct assistance to the Zimbabwean government.

### A fragile transition

For many Zimbabweans, the confrontation over Bennett and the arrest of the magistrate underscore the uncertainty surrounding the country’s political future.

While the unity government raised hopes that Zimbabwe might emerge from years of crisis, the latest developments suggest that rival power centers continue to compete for control.

The central question now is whether the High Court’s authority will be respected — and whether the power-sharing government can survive repeated clashes over the rule of law.

If the magistrate’s arrest is not reversed or explained, analysts say it could become a defining moment in Zimbabwe’s post-election transition: a sign that even under a unity government, the country’s courts remain vulnerable when their decisions collide with political interests.
